prolix

/PROH-liks/ - the stress falls on PROH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Prolix means so tediously long-winded that the words outnumber the ideas.

The minutes of the garden society run prolix under its current secretary: last month's vote on mulch fills nine pages, complete with weather.

Example

The star witness turned out to be hopelessly prolix: asked to confirm the time of the crash, he supplied the bus schedule's history, a defense of his own punctuality, and, four minutes in, the time. The judge began consulting a kitchen timer.

Prolix describes speech or writing that is tediously long-winded — not merely long. An epic can run a thousand pages without being prolix; a two-line email can manage it. The test is whether the words outnumber the ideas, and how hard the reader must dig.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

long-winded: Long-winded is the everyday word for taking forever to reach the point — the after-dinner speech that circles its toast for ten minutes. Prolix means the same fault in a reviewer's register, and it adds a verdict: the length has become tedious, the words outnumbering the ideas.

rambling: Rambling talk wanders off the path as well as taking too long on it — one story drifts into three others. Prolix writing can stay perfectly on its subject and still exhaust you: the fault prolix names is tedious length, not lost direction.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

crisp: snapped clean to the point

compact: packed tight, with no spare words

Where it sits · how far the talking overruns its point

chatty → wordy → prolix

chatty vs. prolix: Chatty is friendly overflow, easily forgiven; it sits at the mild end, well short of prolix.

wordy vs. prolix: Wordy goes further than chatty — the sentences are now carrying fat — but prolix tops the ladder: long-windedness so tedious that readers start skipping.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pro: forward, forth (Latin)

Root — lix: flowed (Latin liquere, to be fluid)

Put it together: Latin prolixus meant 'poured forth': pro- ('forward') plus a form of liquere, 'to flow' — the root that gives us liquid. Prolix speech is language with the tap left running: it flows on and on, well past the point where anyone wanted more.

Use the root in a new word: liquefy: Heat the honey gently and it will liquefy, flowing off the spoon in a slow ribbon.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / critical

Prolix is the reviewer's scalpel for tedious length in words. Verbose, in this unit's reference list, means much the same with a plainer face; long-winded is the kitchen-table version; and turgid — this unit's other style complaint — attacks inflation and pomp rather than sheer length. A text can be turgid in two sentences and prolix across two volumes.
